ASTS Stock Edges Up Overnight: Retail Traders Seize On T-Mobile Dropping Starlink Name From Satellite Page
T-Mobile apparently removed Starlink’s name from its main T-Satellite consumer page but has not announced a change in satellite providers.
In this photo illustration, an AST SpaceMobile logo is seen displayed on a smartphone and in the background. (Photo Illustration by Avishek Das/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon formalized a satellite JV last week to reduce coverage gaps and expand provider options.
The JV preserves existing satellite agreements, including AST’s relationships with AT&T and Verizon.
AST reported over 60 mobile-operator partnerships and about $1.3 billion in contracted revenue backlog in August.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Shares of AST SpaceMobile, Inc. (ASTS) climbed nearly 1% overnight late Sunday as retail investors connected T-Mobile’s removal of Starlink branding from its consumer satellite-service website with a newly formalized alliance among the three largest U.S. wireless carriers.
ASTS stock rose 2% on Friday to close at $58.45, but ended the week down 5%, extending its losing streak to four weeks and marking its worst weekly performance in over a month.
T-Mobile Removes Starlink Name From Consumer Site
T-Mobile quietly removed “with Starlink” from the T-Satellite logo and introductory statement on its main consumer website, PCMag reported on Friday. The page apparently no longer named SpaceX or Starlink Mobile, and T-Mobile had not explained the change. Stocktwits independently confirmed that the main T-Satellite consumer page no longer displays “With Starlink” in its branding.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
The edit drew attention because Starlink powers T-Mobile’s satellite-to-phone service, which connects compatible phones in areas without conventional cellular coverage.
PCMag reported that Starlink references remained on support and business pages. T-Mobile’s business materials also retain the Starlink name and tell customers they may see “T-Mobile SpaceX” or “T-Sat+Starlink” when connected. The distinction matters for AST investors: T-Mobile changed how it presents the service to consumers, but has not announced that it is replacing the network behind it.
Big 3 Satellite JV Preserves Existing AST Deals
The branding report comes shortly after last week’s announcement that AT&T (T), T-Mobile US (TMUS) and Verizon Communications (VZ) had entered a joint-venture agreement, advancing a plan first outlined in May.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
The venture aims to pool limited spectrum resources, improve satellite connectivity in areas without reliable cellular coverage and establish common technical specifications. Wireless-industry veteran Paul Roth will serve as interim CEO while the partners search for a permanent leader.
The carriers said their combined investment would expand provider options and improve direct-to-device access, allowing ordinary phones to connect with satellites. They also said more satellite providers would gain opportunities to compete.
For AST, a key provision protects its existing carrier relationships: the announcement says current carrier-satellite agreements will remain in place and the partners can pursue connectivity efforts independently.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
AST’s Carrier Network Offers Potential Advantage
AST’s business model centers on working with mobile operators to extend their networks into areas that towers cannot reach. This approach makes the venture’s emphasis on shared spectrum and multiple suppliers important for the company’s commercial ambitions.
AST SpaceMobile already has agreements with AT&T and Verizon. Its definitive Verizon agreement, announced in October last year, combines AST’s satellite network with Verizon’s 850 MHz spectrum to provide connectivity when needed, with service targeted to begin in 2026.
AST welcomed the original JV proposal in August, saying that it expected the initiative to help enable space-based cellular broadband connectivity across the U.S. The company also reported partnerships with more than 60 mobile operators covering over 3 billion subscribers and $1.3 billion in contracted revenue backlog from commercial partners and U.S. government awards.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
ASTS Retail Bulls Connect The T-Mobile Dots
T-Mobile’s branding change and the carrier alliance drew discussion on Stocktwits over the weekend, with some ASTS investors viewing them as a potential opening for the company. Sentiment for ASTS on the platform jumped to ‘bullish’ from ‘neutral’ levels a week ago amid a 59% jump in 24-hour message volumes.
ASTS sentiment and message volume as of October 5 | Source: Stocktwits
One user shared the branding report and said, “Buckle up on an official announcement.” The same user also said that Starlink had shifted “from Partner to competitor for T-Mobile,” interpreting the developments as a possible change in carrier allegiance.
Another user called the JV announcement “big news” that “went unnoticed,” highlighting competitive pressure from Starlink. A separate user included “T-Mobile suddenly scrubs Starlink branding” among potential AST catalysts and said, “Something is cooking at $ASTS.”

Verizon, T-Mobile, AT&T From JV to Help Eliminate 'Dead Zones' in US
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 10:07 AM PDT 2 min read
Verizon Communications (VZ), T-Mobile US (TMUS) and AT&T (T) have established a joint venture aimed at boosting mobile network services in underserved areas and eliminating "dead zones" in the country, the companies said Thursday.
In May, the three companies reached an agreement in principle to form a new JV and said they would pool limited spectrum resources to help eliminate coverage "dead zones" and expand satellite coverage for customers.
"Through combined investment by the three JV partners, provider options will expand, and, as a first step, direct-to-device access will improve," Verizon, T-Mobile and AT&T said Thursday. "This will enhance competition as consumer choices grow in satellite service."
The venture also aims to provide other customer benefits, such as helping make redundant connectivity available when existing ground-based networks are not available due to extreme natural disasters and almost eliminating "dead zones" in the country currently without mobile service.
"More satellite service providers will gain opportunities to compete, invest, and grow and the JV will work with rural mobile network operators to enable them to bring new products to market for their customers," the statement said.
Wireless industry veteran Paul Roth will be the JV's interim chief executive until a permanent CEO is appointed. A board with representatives from each founding member will manage the venture, according to the statement.
Existing carrier-satellite deals will remain intact, the companies said, adding that the JV partners will be able to continue connectivity efforts independently.
Earlier this week, AT&T and Corning (GLW) announced a multiyear agreement valued at more than $3 billion, under which Corning will provide fiber and cable needed for AT&T's network expansion amid strong data demand spurred by the expanding use of artificial intelligence.
Last month, Verizon and Corning struck a multi-billion-dollar deal for more than 80 million miles of high-density optical fiber and connectivity solutions from 2027 through 2032 in order to meet strong consumer broadband demand.

T-Mobile 2025 Corporate Responsibility Report: Designing for Accessibility and Building Industry-wide Best Practices
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 6:35 AM PDT 3 min read
NORTHAMPTON, MA / ACCESS Newswire / October 6, 2026 / Expanding access to connectivity means ensuring that all customers, regardless of their ability, can use our products and services. We offer a range of accessibility options, including Speech-to-Speech and IP Relay services for calls, American Sign Language-fluent customer service specialists, and access to enhanced 411 resources. In retail stores, we host Accessibility Days to provide specialized assistance to customers with disabilities.
T-Mobile's Accessibility Resource Center (ARC) helps us embed accessibility into products and services from the start. The ARC team provides guidance on accessible product development, including training materials and policies, and increases digital accessibility awareness across our workforce. In 2025, the ARC team launched a comprehensive reporting and accountability program that shares compliance and performance accessibility insights with internal teams and vendors responsible for developing front-end content.
We champion accessibility beyond T-Mobile's walls. Our ARC team has developed and maintained MagentaA11y, a free, open-source tool that allows users to design, build, and improve the accessibility of web and native development and design elements. It provides acceptance criteria, code samples, developer guidance, videos, and testing instructions to support accessibility throughout the development process. In 2025, MagentaA11y was redesigned to enhance user experience, resulting in more than 40,000 interactions worldwide, including adoption from other companies leveraging the open-source framework to develop customized accessibility solutions. In recognition of its impact, T-Mobile's ARC team received the 2025 GAADY Award from the Global Accessibility Awareness Day (GAAD) Foundation for MagentaA11y's contribution to advancing digital inclusion.
To advance accessibility within T-Mobile and beyond, we turn to leaders across the industry. In 2025, the ARC team facilitated the PNW Accessibility Professionals Meetup, bringing together over 125 experts from more than 30 tech companies in Seattle and Portland to share insights, best practices, and innovations in accessibility quarterly. For employees, we held an annual Digital Accessibility Summit, drawing over 1,800 attendees and offering educational sessions alongside interactive experiences. Beyond these events, T-Mobile partners with accessibility-focused organizations, including Disability:IN, American Council of the Blind, American Foundation for the Blind, and the GAAD Foundation, to expand community outreach and support broader accessibility initiatives.
Inside T-Mobile's Accessibility Lab The Accessibility Lab at T-Mobile's Bellevue headquarters reinforces accessibility as a core consideration in product and digital design, providing T-Mobile employees with hands-on experiences that reflect how people with disabilities interact with technology, including simulations of hearing loss, screen readers, and refreshable braille displays. Designed as an immersive learning environment, The Accessibility Lab enables employees to ask questions, build understanding, and better recognize the real-world impact of their work on people with disabilities. Throughout 2025, employees and internal teams participated in guided tours and learning sessions focused on digital accessibility. Beyond our workforce, we welcomed colleagues from external organizations seeking to develop their own accessibility labs, extending the Lab's impact beyond T-Mobile. Through this hands-on, collaborative approach, this initiative helps foster a shared commitment to inclusive design and a more accessible digital experience for all.

T-Mobile Announces Planned Chief Financial Officer Transition
Jessica Uhl Appointed CFO Designate; To Succeed Peter Osvaldik as Chief Financial Officer in February 2027
Peter Osvaldik to Continue as CFO Through a Transition Period Before Assuming a Strategic Advisor Role Until His Planned July 1, 2027
BELLEVUE, Wash. — Thursday, September 3, 2026 — T-Mobile US,
Inc. (NASDAQ: TMUS) today announced that Jessica Uhl will join the company as CFO Designate and succeed Peter Osvaldik as Chief Financial Officer in February 2027, as part of the company’s long-term leadership succession planning. The
announcement follows Osvaldik’s previous one-year contract extension to support the CEO transition.
former Chief Financial Officer of Shell and most recently President of GE Vernova, will join T-Mobile as CFO Designate effective mid-September. Uhl will work alongside
current Chief Financial Officer Peter Osvaldik during an extended transition period and will succeed him as CFO in February 2027. Osvaldik will then assume a Strategic Advisor role until his planned retirement from
T-Mobile at the conclusion of his contract on July 1, 2027.
Uhl brings extensive financial and strategic
leadership experience from a 30-year career leading large-scale global businesses and prudently allocating capital. As CFO of Shell, one of the world’s largest and most complex enterprises, she oversaw
financial strategy, capital markets execution and investor relations across a business operating in more than 70 countries. She developed and led emerging businesses across Shell’s diverse portfolio, spanning infrastructure, commodity and
consumer markets.
Most recently, as President of GE Vernova, Uhl oversaw corporate development, strategy, ventures research and development, as well as
the company’s generative AI program. Her experience leading through transformation, allocating capital at scale, scaling new businesses and deploying emerging technologies, positions her to partner with
T-Mobile’s leadership team as the company advances its next era of disruption, profitable growth and innovation.
“I am thrilled to welcome Jessica to T-Mobile,” said Srini Gopalan, President and CEO of T-Mobile. “She brings deep financial and strategic acumen, capital allocation expertise and an innovative growth mindset that is a perfect fit for T-Mobile’s next
era. Jessica has a distinguished track record leading complex businesses, effectively balancing strategic investments with financial and operational discipline. After a thorough search process, I am confident Jessica is the right leader to help
shape our growth agenda as CFO, and I am grateful she and Peter will collaborate through an extended transition period to ensure continuity and a seamless succession.”
Osvaldik joined T-Mobile in 2016 and has served as Chief Financial Officer since 2020. He will continue as CFO through
February 2027, when he will assume a Strategic Advisor role until his planned retirement. The transition is designed to provide continuity across T-Mobile’s financial organization, investor and capital
markets relationships, and broader strategic priorities, while enabling a seamless transfer of leadership and institutional knowledge. Osvaldik’s tenure as CFO has been defined by disciplined financial stewardship, consistent financial
outperformance, and an unwavering commitment to T-Mobile’s mission.
“Peter’s legacy at T-Mobile is extraordinary,”
added Gopalan. “Over more than a decade with the company, his financial rigor, strategic clarity and care for our mission have helped build T-Mobile into the dynamic, innovative and customer-obsessed
company it is today. The strong financial foundation Peter has solidified will help propel T-Mobile into its next chapter of growth and expansion. I am deeply grateful for Peter’s partnership and his
continued commitment to T-Mobile, from extending his contract to support my transition to CEO to helping ensure continuity as we welcome Jessica and prepare for our next chapter. We wish him the very best in
his well-earned retirement.
“T-Mobile is entering a period of extraordinary opportunity,” Gopalan
concluded. “We have a long growth runway to continue our leadership in consumer wireless by bringing America’s Best Network to more customers in small markets and rural areas and winning network seekers; accelerating our growth beyond
consumer wireless to broadband, T-Mobile for Business and new adjacencies; and further strengthening the customer differentiation that defines this company. Jessica will be a critical strategic and operational
partner as we execute with focus, scale our ambitions and create lasting value for customers, employees and shareholders.”
T-Mobile reaffirms its previously stated 2026 financial guidance and maintains its capital return program and long-term financial framework.
About T-Mobile US, Inc.
T-Mobile US, Inc. (NASDAQ: TMUS) is America’s supercharged Un-carrier,
delivering an advanced 4G LTE and transformative nationwide 5G network that will offer reliable connectivity for all. T-Mobile’s customers benefit from its unmatched combination of value and quality,
unwavering obsession with offering them the best possible service experience, and undisputable drive for disruption that creates competition and innovation in wireless, broadband and beyond. Based in Bellevue, Wash.,
T-Mobile provides services through its subsidiaries and operates its flagship brands, T-Mobile and Metro by T-Mobile. For more
information, please visit htt ps://w ww.t-mobile.com.

Q2 Results, Alongside Record-High Wireless NPS Score, Another Proof Point that the Un-carrier’s Winning Formula of Best Network, Best Value and Best Experiences Drives Durable and Profitable Growth
Continued Strong Account Growth and Deepening Customer Relationships Fueled by Widening Differentiation

Bellevue, WA — July 23, 2026 — T-Mobile US, Inc. (NASDAQ: TMUS) reported second quarter 2026 results today, delivering strong postpaid net account and postpaid ARPA growth. The company’s robust account and ARPA growth contributed to industry-leading service revenue growth, including Postpaid service revenue growth, strong Net income, industry-leading Core Adjusted EBITDA growth, strong Net cash provided by operating activities margin and industry-leading Adjusted Free Cash Flow margin.
“Q2 marked another strong quarter of execution as we continued making meaningful progress toward our ambitious 2026 and 2027 objectives, including achieving our highest-ever wireless NPS score of 46,” said Srini Gopalan, CEO of T-Mobile. “Our strategy is simple: give customers the best network, the best value, and the best experience, all in one place. That’s how we eliminate trade-offs for our customers, and that’s what sets us apart, and our results represent another proof point that our strategy is working. Our differentiated approach is all about creating durable growth opportunities that no one else in the industry can match. As our unmatched value proposition continues to resonate with customers, and as we continue to invest in our network and our technology, we see a tremendous runway for growth across both wireless and broadband, as well as new businesses. We’re just getting started.”

Can AI Really Disrupt DoorDash (DASH)? Jim Cramer Isn’t Convinced
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 2:00 PM PDT 3 min read
During the September 29 episode of Mad Money, Jim Cramer pointed to DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) as a prime example of a market overreaction to theoretical software threats, as he commented:
How about the food delivery services? Look, this isn't the first time DoorDash has gotten hit on AI displacement worries. Seven months ago, an outfit called Citrini Research published a doomsday fiction piece about how AI agents would make this business obsolete. The stock got crushed at the time, but then managed a fabulous comeback; 150 went to 240.
You can also read why DoorDash, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:DASH) $300 million Grubhub deal may matter more for its moat than near-term earnings here.
Jim Cramer Says the Chip Shortage “Can’t Be Solved” Without KLAC
Logistics Infrastructure and Marketplace Scale
DoorDash, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:DASH) operational thesis is backed by dominant market metrics that show the depth of its physical and technological moat. Controlling roughly 67% of the U.S. meal delivery market, the company routes millions of orders daily across a network of more than 900,000 partner merchant locations and a large number of Dashers. The scale is further supported by a growing subscriber base exceeding 35 million active DashPass and Wolt+ members, who generate predictable, high-frequency order flow and higher average order values.
While autonomous AI agents can automate front-end order placement or comparative price discovery, they cannot execute the complex physical routing, real-time localized batching, and point-of-sale integration required to move physical goods. Rather than replacing the core infrastructure, AI consumer agents must route fulfillment requests directly through DoorDash's software interfaces, effectively converting potential AI disintermediators into top-of-funnel demand sources. Furthermore, the company's ongoing expansion into non-restaurant verticals, such as grocery, convenience, and retail, combined with a high-margin advertising platform that generates over $1 billion in annual run-rate revenue, continues to drive unit economic efficiency and widen the competitive gap against smaller aggregators.
Valuation Multiples, Margin Expansion, and Downside Risks
With a forward price-to-earnings ratio near 38x, DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) maintains a valuation premium over broader consumer discretionary benchmarks and traditional marketplace peers. The premium is anchored by strong top-line momentum, expanding adjusted EBITDA margins, and a positive GAAP net income trajectory following years of heavy operational investment.
However, such an elevated multiple leaves little margin for execution errors or macro shocks. Major downside risks include potential regulatory shifts around gig-worker classification and minimum wage mandates in major metropolitan markets, rising courier acquisition costs, and potential softening in discretionary consumer spending. If order frequency or active user growth slows, the stock's premium valuation could face sharp multiple compression.
Hedge Fund Positioning and Short Sentiment
According to Insider Monkey's database, 107 hedge funds held positions in DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) at the close of the second quarter, down from 117 funds in the prior quarter. Newlands Management Operations LLC was the company's most prominent shareholder among the hedge funds tracked by Insider Monkey, with over 7 million shares. Short seller activity remains limited, with short interest standing at 4.01% of the float as of September 15.
Cramer's bullish thesis rests on the premise that Wall Street repeatedly underestimates the durability of real-world fulfillment networks. With DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) generating expanding free cash flow and maintaining its multi-category market lead, its physical distribution and merchant network continue to provide a durable buffer against software tools attempting to bypass the platform.

The New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) announced a historic $131.5 million enforcement action against DoorDash for systematic violations of the local Delivery Worker Laws.
The settlement will place more than $115 million directly into the pockets of delivery workers and pay for $16 million in civil penalties and costs. More than 260,000 workers were underpaid by DoorDash, including workers who were not paid at all, or were paid late for work they had already performed.
It’s the largest worker settlement in New York City history.
“DoorDash underpaid more than 260,000 workers, and today we are getting that money back,” said Mayor Mamdani. “When a worker earns a wage, they deserve to be paid that wage, on time and in full.”
He reminded the public that no corporation is above the law—especially when it earns $13.7 billion in revenue, like DoorDash did in 2025, a 28% increase compared to their 2024 revenue of $10.72 billion.
“Today, New York City’s delivery workers are showing that opaque algorithms will not have the final word when it comes to how much they are paid for the hard work they do,” said DCWP Commissioner Samuel A.A. Levine.
The settlement is about more than recovering money that workers are owed. It also puts in place a new monitoring system ensuring DoorDash follows the law going forward—one that gives workers a direct role in identifying violations and gives the City data it needs to act.
A Princeton University partner, the Workers’ Algorithm Observatory, will develop software that will allow the drivers to share their DoorDash trip and earnings data directly with the agency. It will allow DCWP to monitor DoorDash’s compliance with minimum pay, maximum trip distances, trip disclosures, pay transparency, and tip transparency.
DCWP’s citywide investigation began after dozens of workers filed reports with the Department.
The agency found that DoorDash failed to pay thousands of workers at all for work they had performed and failed to pay thousands more on time. These workers will receive compensation calculated at approximately 200% of the amount they were underpaid.
For example, a worker who was owed $1,000 but received no payment will receive $3,000. A worker who was paid $1,000 later than allowed under the law will receive $2,000.
Workers don’t even need to file a claim or submit evidence to receive payment. DCWP has identified all individuals owed money through its analysis of DoorDash’s records—and payments will be sent out this fall.

The case’s Settlement Administrator will send personalized emails to each worker who experienced an underpayment from April 22, 2022 to June 28, 2026. Workers will be able to choose between an electronic payment and a check by mail.
More details of the case is available at nyc.gov/doordash.
As part of the investigation, DCWP obtained terabytes of data from DoorDash, including billions of rows documenting the company’s treatment of delivery workers. DCWP’s Research and Analytics Division analyzed the data to identify more than 152 million individual payment transactions and 110 million working hours connected to the investigation.
DoorDash will be required to make software updates to prevent the company from offering a delivery to a worker in New York City unless that worker’s time is being recorded as compensable on-call time or trip time. The updates will also provide workers with additional information about their work time and pay and ensure DoorDash complies with the Minimum Pay Rule for “batched” trips, ending the unlawful practice of paying a lower rate for certain legs of a trip.
“Amidst a cost of living crisis, delivery workers deserve to rest assured that work completed means compensation earned,” said Council Member and Consumer and Worker Protection Chair Harvey Epstein.
The city passed a minimum wage law in 2021 which is adjusted annually for inflation and currently sits at $22.13 per hour.
“DoorDash thought they could shortchange their workers and get away with it,” said Council Member Sandy Nurse. “As DoorDash pulls in record profits, the workers who make them rich are entitled to their fair share.”

DoorDash launches retail returns service, self-designed drones
DoorDash Air is a new drone delivery service that the company will operate using its own self-built aircraft rather than an outside supplier. (Photo: DoorDash)
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 10:03 AM PDT 5 min read
DoorDash is entering the reverse logistics market and leaning heavily into drone delivery, announcing on Wednesday that it has launched a new retail returns service and a custom-built drone delivery system for time-sensitive orders in another modal expansion of its last-mile logistics network.
They were among a series of product releases and enhancements, unveiled at a big user event, aimed at making shopping and ordering food, grocery and retail items more convenient.
The returns program is live in select cities and is expected to roll out nationwide in November using the same gig driver pool that delivers from stores to homes, the tech platform said. Consumers pay a flat $7.99 for Dasher Returns — no box or label required. DoorDash (NASDAQ: DASH) said drivers will pick up return orders in as fast as 30 minutes and return them to the store, which will process the return and issue a refund within days.
By offering returns, DoorDash is moving into a space that offers higher margins than store-to-door delivery and taking on parcel shipping incumbents like FedEx and UPS that are focusing more on returns than short-distance delivery in the B2C e-commerce market. FedEx last year began offering a lower cost version of its no-box, no-label returns to make it easier for customers to return unwanted merchandise, but the service requires consumers to drop off the goods at outlets such as FedEx Office and Kohl's store locations.
Earlier this year, Uber Eats introduced a service that allows customers to return goods ordered through its app for a fee.
But it's an open question whether consumers are willing to pay for returns when there is less urgency than with an inbound order and they can wait to drop it off at a store themselves for free.
"For retailers, it means turning the stores they already have into a growth channel, not a warehouse three states away," said Chief Revenue Officer Shanna Prevé in a news release.
Meanwhile, DoorDash has added to the growing number of retailers who have linked their product catalogs to its marketplace. Shoppers can now use the DoorDash app to order goods from Macy's, Anthropologie, The North Face, Vans and Timberland and receive fast delivery. Costco and Skims began delivery partnerships with DoorDash earlier this month.
DoorDash calls its retail product "Mall-in-Your-Pocket" because consumers can shop for apparel, beauty and home goods with fast delivery from hundreds of stores nationwide on one platform.
DoorDash also recently introduced new ways for retailers and brands to grow. Brand Center gives participating brands real-time visibility into inventory on store shelves and shopper substitution trends, helping them understand how their products are showing up in stores and what shoppers choose when an item is unavailable.
DoorDash also said it is investing in its own drone delivery operation, offering customers a faster delivery option from local restaurants and convenience stores.
The delivery platform's in-house robotics and automation division, DoorDash Labs, made the six-rotor drones on its own. Until now, DoorDash has relied on outside drone operators like Alphabet's Wing and Flytrex to conduct the actual aerial deliveries. Lowe's, for example, this month began a pilot program for drone delivery in North Carolina enabled by the DoorDash marketplace and Wing's small, unmanned aerial vehicles.
"We'll continue our partnership with third parties like Wing and Flytrex, but in the same way we use multiple delivery methods, having multiple drone delivery options adds resilience to our network and helps us better serve merchants and bring the benefits of drone delivery to more communities faster," said spokesman Eli Scheinholtz in an email exchange.
DoorDash said it closely consulted with businesses to design everything from packaging, to loading systems and ground handoffs. It is building an array of loading options designed to fit into existing business operations and make drone delivery feasible for local businesses of all sizes.
About 80% of typical DoorDash restaurant orders are light and small enough for the aircraft to carry safely.
"Any local business should be able to reach consumers by air. We built the whole system so that they can deliver by air without being disruptive to how they run their business," said Harrison Shih, head of DoorDash Air, in the announcement.
Trial flights are underway in Northern California with national brands Chipotle and Popeyes, and local restaurants. Delivery times have averaged less than five minutes so far, DoorDash said.
Customers can choose on the app whether their order is delivered by a driver, its self-designed small robot or a drone. An autonomous system uses smart routing, incorporating factors like weather, flight range, and ground traffic to narrow down which orders actually make sense to send by air. Using the app, customers can select whether a driver, a Dot robot or a drone is the best delivery option.
The drone's cruising noise is similar to that of a passing car. Orders are picked up and lowered to the ground with a winch, with a backup option to safely lower the aircraft to the ground in rare events, DoorDash said. Amazon drones, by contrast, drop boxes at their destination from about 13 feet in the air.
In other news, DoorDash also introduced text ordering, allowing customers to simply send a text describing what they want from a restaurant or grocery store without the need to fiddle with an app or browser.
Why It Matters: DoorDash is a giant platform that is leveraging its technology to push more and more into retail parcel delivery and becoming a competitor to other courier companies.

Inside DoorDash’s Push to Connect Every Restaurant Channel
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 9:04 AM PDT 4 min read
This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt.
DashOS is meant to link marketplace discovery with future transactions.
DoorDash wants to become more than a delivery marketplace for restaurants.
Its new DashOS platform connects ordering, reservations, loyalty, customer data, and marketing. The goal is to help restaurants recognize the same guest across delivery, direct ordering, and dine-in visits, then use that information to bring the customer back.
That is difficult for many operators today. Guests move easily between channels, but their activity often lands in separate systems. One person can appear to be several unrelated customers, leaving restaurants without a clear picture of what led to another purchase.
Restaurants also have to oversee numerous technology products in addition to running their kitchens and dining rooms. DoorDash data shows 40 percent of surveyed U.S. operators use four to five systems, and 83 percent believe better-connected technology would improve profitability.
"The idea is really to become the growth partner for merchants, period, and be the one-stop shop for merchants to look to when they say I wanna grow," says Parisa Sadrzadeh, DoorDash's vice president of strategy and operations.
DoorDash introduced DashOS during its Dash Forward 2026 event. The platform connects DoorDash Marketplace with the company's direct ordering, loyalty, reservation, and marketing products.
Customers must opt into a restaurant's loyalty program or agree to share their information for marketing. Once they do, the restaurant can see eligible activity across the DoorDash products it uses and communicate with that customer directly.
DoorDash sees its marketplace as the starting point for many of those relationships. A customer might discover a restaurant through delivery, return through its website, and later visit in person. DashOS is designed to connect those transactions instead of treating each one as a separate relationship.
The early loyalty results provide DoorDash's clearest evidence for the model. More than one in five customers who visit the DoorDash page of a participating restaurant enroll in its loyalty program. Those members order 1.8 times as often and spend approximately 1.75 times as much per person as customers who have not enrolled.
DashOS can use purchasing history to recommend menu items and support marketing through email, text messages and push notifications. Campaigns can run automatically for restaurants without dedicated marketing employees, or operators can customize them.
The information can follow customers to a restaurant's direct ordering site. Once logged in, a customer can see previous DoorDash orders, receive recommendations, and use saved payment information. DoorDash can also provide delivery for the direct order.
Reservations are another piece of the customer record. DoorDash said AI-powered recommendations increased total bookings by more than 15 percent in early tests. SevenRooms marketing products using blinded, aggregated DoorDash Marketplace information have produced more than $150 million in restaurant sales this year. DoorDash acquired SevenRooms in 2025.
The platform works with technology restaurants already use. DoorDash is expanding connections with Clover, Qu, Checkmate, Chowly, Deliverect, Stream and UrbanPiper. Starting in 2027, more than 80,000 restaurants using those providers are expected to gain access to SevenRooms customer profiles, online ordering, in-store rewards and omnichannel loyalty products.
DoorDash still has work to do to make the products operate as one system. The company has connected its merchant portal more closely with its customer relationship software and plans more automation.
"The idea is to simplify this into one platform," Sadrzadeh says. "We need to continue to improve it and continue to simplify it."
DashOS is one piece of DoorDash's effort to play a larger role in local commerce. The company also introduced a service that lets customers order through text messages.
U.S. consumers using iPhones can join a waitlist for the beta. A customer can text DoorDash with a specific request, ask for a local recommendation, or request a usual order. The system searches nearby restaurants, builds a suggested cart, and handles checkout inside the conversation. It can also remember preferences and order modifications.
The service builds on Ask DoorDash, the company's in-app ordering assistant. DoorDash said customers have used the assistant to discover more than 40,000 restaurants. Nearly half of restaurant orders placed through it went to businesses those customers had not tried previously.
DoorDash also introduced DoorDash Air, an autonomous delivery system scheduled to begin pilot service in Northern California with Chipotle, Popeyes and local restaurants.
The company designed the aircraft, packaging, and loading process using historical order information and existing kitchen workflows. Roughly 80 percent of typical restaurant orders on DoorDash are light and small enough for the aircraft to carry safely, depending on travel distance and operating conditions.
Early tests produced average travel times of less than five minutes from a restaurant to a customer's door. DoorDash's Autonomous Delivery Platform chooses whether a driver, Dot delivery robot, or drone is the best option for each eligible order. The decision accounts for distance, weight, weather, traffic, and kitchen preparation time.
The Dash Forward event also included retail returns, AI assistance for drivers, and a connector that can bring DoorDash ordering into compatible workplace AI products.

DoorDash’s $300 Million Grubhub Deal Opens a New Venue-Commerce Opportunity
DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) is acquiring Wonder's Grubhub Campus Dining business for $300 million and investing another $125 million in Wonder's Series D. The campus business operates at more than 450 colleges and universities, allowing students to order from campus dining facilities, pay with dining dollars, and schedule pickup. DoorDash plans to expand the technology beyond campuses into stadiums, hotels and similar venues, with the transaction expected to close in the first half of 2027.
The deal fits DoorDash's broader push beyond conventional restaurant delivery. Its Q2 2026 Marketplace GOV rose 36% to $33.1 billion, while orders increased 27% to 970 million. Even excluding Deliveroo, GOV growth was still 23%, showing that DoorDash has meaningful underlying momentum to support new verticals.
DoorDash’s $300 Million Grubhub Deal Opens a New Venue-Commerce Opportunity
Strong Cash Generation Supports DoorDash's Latest Expansion Bet
The strongest upside is the potential to turn an established campus ordering network into a broader venue-commerce platform. With more than 450 universities already using the technology, DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) is acquiring an existing merchant and consumer infrastructure rather than building a campus product from scratch. Extending that vertically integrated ordering and pickup system into stadiums, hotels, and other controlled environments could increase order density and create additional Commerce Platform revenue without relying entirely on traditional restaurant delivery.
The $300 million purchase is also relatively modest against DoorDash's financial scale. The company generated $742 million of free cash flow in Q2 alone, up from $355 million a year earlier, while adjusted EBITDA reached $914 million, up 40%. That gives DoorDash capacity to fund the acquisition without putting significant pressure on near-term liquidity.
The Wonder investment adds another strategic option. Wonder has expanded to 157 locations, more than quadrupling its footprint since early 2025, while investing in robotics and AI. DoorDash therefore gains exposure to technology that could eventually improve food preparation, fulfillment, and delivery economics, potentially supporting longer-term margin expansion if automation becomes commercially viable.
The Deal's Near-Term Earnings Impact Could Remain Limited
The immediate financial contribution from Grubhub Campus Dining is unlikely to be material relative to DoorDash's existing scale. DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) generated $4.45 billion of revenue and $33.1 billion of Marketplace GOV in Q2, meaning the $300 million acquisition is strategically significant but unlikely by itself to materially change consolidated earnings. The larger valuation argument depends on successfully expanding the campus technology into new venues, something that remains unproven.
There is also execution risk from expanding into businesses with different operating requirements. DoorDash is already investing heavily in its global technology platform and international operations, while Q2 research and development expense rose to $535 million from $351 million a year earlier. Adding a new venue-focused platform could increase spending before the economics of stadiums, hotels and other locations are established.
The $125 million Wonder investment carries an additional risk because Wonder remains in an aggressive expansion phase. Its footprint has quadrupled since the start of 2025, and it plans to enter Texas in 2027. DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) is therefore committing capital to a business pursuing physical expansion and robotics investment whose returns may take years to materialize.
The partnership is strategically positive for DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) because it expands the company into controlled, high-density venues while adding technology that could be reused beyond college campuses. DoorDash's 23% organic GOV growth, rising adjusted EBITDA, and $742 million quarterly free cash flow provide a strong financial foundation for the move.
However, the $300 million acquisition is unlikely to materially affect near-term earnings, making the investment case dependent on DoorDash successfully scaling the platform into stadiums, hotels, and other venues. The deal therefore strengthens DoorDash's long-term growth optionality more than its immediate financial outlook.

DoorDash announced on Wednesday that it’s launching a text-to-order AI agent that lets users place orders through Apple Messages. The new tool allows users to send prompts like “order my usual,” and the agent will understand that they mean their Friday night order.
DoorDash says users can also ask for a specific dish and request a local recommendation. The agent will then search local spots and suggest a cart based on the prompt, and even text photos of the food it recommends. When ordering for a group, DoorDash says the agent can handle mixed dietary preferences and different quantities in one order.
By launching an AI agent for food ordering, DoorDash is looking to gain an edge over rivals Uber Eats and Grubhub. The launch also comes amid a growing push to adopt personal AI agents that can handle tasks without requiring users to navigate apps or websites themselves.
DoorDash is opening up a waitlist for users in the U.S. to try out the new feature.
In addition to the new AI agent, DoorDash announced that it will begin testing its delivery drones with select restaurants in Northern California.

DoorDash Debuts Returns Program Amid New Retail Partnerships
DoorDash launched a returns program along with an expansion of its retail marketplace, according to a Wednesday (Sept. 30) press release.
The expansion involves partnerships in the apparel, beauty and home spaces, with Macy’s, Anthropologie, The North Face, Vans and Timberland now available options to customers, the release said.
“This is what we mean by the mall in your pocket: the brands you already know and trust, on the shelf near you, delivered as easily as walking into the mall used to be,” DoorDash Chief Revenue Officer Shanna Prevé said in the release. “You can get Macy’s or Anthropologie in as little as an hour and return it just as easily if it’s not right, no box, no label, back on the shelf and the money back in your pocket. For retailers, it means turning the stores they already have into a growth channel, not a warehouse three states away.”

The returns are possible via Dasher Returns, which lets consumers pay a flat $7.99 fee to schedule a return for an eligible retail order, and a Dasher can retrieve it from their door in as quickly as 30 minutes and bring it back to the store, according to the release. Pricing and times are subject to change.
“The return is processed on the spot, the item can go directly back on the shelf, and the consumer receives their refund within days,” the release said.
DoorDash also announced several other products and services Wednesday as it held its Dash Forward 2026 event.
These include the ability to place orders with DoorDash by sending a text rather than using an app or browser; the ability to connect DoorDash to compatible internal AI tools so employees can order team lunches or items for office restocking; a platform called DoorDash OS that connects all the DoorDash tools that are used by restaurants; a new AI assistant called DashBuddy that answers questions for Dashers; and a planned upcoming drone delivery system that will serve local businesses, the company said in several press releases issued Wednesday.
DoorDash last week announced a drone delivery partnership with Lowe’s and Google’s Wing, PYMNTS reported Thursday (Sept. 24).
The move and others like it are giving retailers a way to find out what delivery speed is worth, PYMNTS reported Friday (Sept. 25). More than 20% of orders on the DoorDash platform last year traveled between three and five miles, but those orders took almost 25% longer than shorter deliveries, mainly because pairing them with a driver took longer. Drone-delivered orders arrived in an average of 25 minutes during 2025, while some locations taking part in partner drone pilots saw order volumes grow by around 30%.
“Whether the arithmetic works will depend heavily on cost,” the report said, citing Barclays research showing autonomous delivery costs below that of conventional delivery. “Cutting several dollars from fulfillment does more to improve the economics of delivering a $15 order than a $150 order.”

Can AI Really Disrupt DoorDash (DASH)? Jim Cramer Isn’t Convinced
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 2:00 PM PDT 3 min read
During the September 29 episode of Mad Money, Jim Cramer pointed to DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) as a prime example of a market overreaction to theoretical software threats, as he commented:
How about the food delivery services? Look, this isn't the first time DoorDash has gotten hit on AI displacement worries. Seven months ago, an outfit called Citrini Research published a doomsday fiction piece about how AI agents would make this business obsolete. The stock got crushed at the time, but then managed a fabulous comeback; 150 went to 240.
You can also read why DoorDash, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:DASH) $300 million Grubhub deal may matter more for its moat than near-term earnings here.
Jim Cramer Says the Chip Shortage “Can’t Be Solved” Without KLAC
Logistics Infrastructure and Marketplace Scale
DoorDash, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:DASH) operational thesis is backed by dominant market metrics that show the depth of its physical and technological moat. Controlling roughly 67% of the U.S. meal delivery market, the company routes millions of orders daily across a network of more than 900,000 partner merchant locations and a large number of Dashers. The scale is further supported by a growing subscriber base exceeding 35 million active DashPass and Wolt+ members, who generate predictable, high-frequency order flow and higher average order values.
While autonomous AI agents can automate front-end order placement or comparative price discovery, they cannot execute the complex physical routing, real-time localized batching, and point-of-sale integration required to move physical goods. Rather than replacing the core infrastructure, AI consumer agents must route fulfillment requests directly through DoorDash's software interfaces, effectively converting potential AI disintermediators into top-of-funnel demand sources. Furthermore, the company's ongoing expansion into non-restaurant verticals, such as grocery, convenience, and retail, combined with a high-margin advertising platform that generates over $1 billion in annual run-rate revenue, continues to drive unit economic efficiency and widen the competitive gap against smaller aggregators.
Valuation Multiples, Margin Expansion, and Downside Risks
With a forward price-to-earnings ratio near 38x, DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) maintains a valuation premium over broader consumer discretionary benchmarks and traditional marketplace peers. The premium is anchored by strong top-line momentum, expanding adjusted EBITDA margins, and a positive GAAP net income trajectory following years of heavy operational investment.
However, such an elevated multiple leaves little margin for execution errors or macro shocks. Major downside risks include potential regulatory shifts around gig-worker classification and minimum wage mandates in major metropolitan markets, rising courier acquisition costs, and potential softening in discretionary consumer spending. If order frequency or active user growth slows, the stock's premium valuation could face sharp multiple compression.
Hedge Fund Positioning and Short Sentiment
According to Insider Monkey's database, 107 hedge funds held positions in DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) at the close of the second quarter, down from 117 funds in the prior quarter. Newlands Management Operations LLC was the company's most prominent shareholder among the hedge funds tracked by Insider Monkey, with over 7 million shares. Short seller activity remains limited, with short interest standing at 4.01% of the float as of September 15.
Cramer's bullish thesis rests on the premise that Wall Street repeatedly underestimates the durability of real-world fulfillment networks. With DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) generating expanding free cash flow and maintaining its multi-category market lead, its physical distribution and merchant network continue to provide a durable buffer against software tools attempting to bypass the platform.
While we acknowledge the potential of DASH as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. DoorDash Air combines a new six-propeller aircraft with restaurant loading infrastructure and the company’s existing delivery marketplace
DoorDash has unveiled a purpose-built delivery drone and supporting system for restaurant deliveries. The company will begin piloting DoorDash Air in Northern California.
The announcement provides new details about the aircraft and the infrastructure behind DoorDash’s in-house drone delivery program. DoorDash says the aircraft can handle about 80% of typical restaurant orders on its platform. Initial testing showed average delivery times of under five minutes from the restaurant to the customer’s door.
The program expands DoorDash’s existing drone strategy. The company has already completed tens of thousands of drone deliveries through partnerships with operators including Wing and Flytrex. DoorDash launched its own DoorDash Air program in July after DoorDash Labs received FAA Part 135 air carrier certification.
A Drone Designed Around Restaurant Orders
The new DoorDash aircraft uses six slow-spinning propellers positioned away from the aircraft’s arms to reduce noise. At cruising altitude, DoorDash says its sound is comparable to a passing car.
The aircraft was designed around the size and weight of restaurant orders. DoorDash estimates that about 80% of typical orders are light and small enough for the aircraft to carry safely. The company notes that the estimate comes from a limited sample of U.S. restaurant deliveries.
DoorDash also says initial tests produced average delivery times of less than five minutes between the restaurant and customer. The company cautions that the estimate comes from deliveries of limited distance and size. Delivery times are not guaranteed.
The Northern California pilot will include Chipotle Mexican Grill, Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen and Momo N Curry among its first restaurant partners.
Building the System Around the Restaurant
DoorDash is positioning the aircraft as one part of a larger delivery system. The company has also developed the merchant handoff process, ground infrastructure and software needed to route orders.
The approach addresses a practical challenge for restaurant drone delivery. Restaurants already have established kitchen workflows and limited space. Requiring specialized infrastructure could make drone delivery harder to adopt.
DoorDash says it has developed several loading options that fit into existing restaurant operations. The goal is to let businesses use drone delivery without major changes to their facilities or workflows.
Harrison Shih, Head of DoorDash Air, said the company designed the system around that requirement.
“We didn’t start with a drone and ask what would fit. We started with what people order and how local businesses actually operate, then built the entire system from there.”
The approach also marks a shift from DoorDash’s earlier drone deployments. The company has worked with third-party drone operators while integrating drone delivery into its ordering platform. DoorDash launched service with Flytrex in the Dallas-Fort Worth area in 2025 and has also expanded its partnership with Wing across several U.S. markets.
With DoorDash Air, the company is adding its own aircraft and delivery system while continuing to work with outside drone partners.
DoorDash is integrating DoorDash Air into its Autonomous Delivery Platform, which determines how individual orders should be delivered.
Depending on the order, the platform can select a human Dasher, DoorDash’s Dot delivery robot, a drone or a delivery partner. This allows DoorDash to use drones for orders that fit the aircraft while routing other deliveries through different methods.
DoorDash says its marketplace currently routes about 10 million orders each day. That volume gives the platform a large pool of deliveries from which to identify orders suited to autonomous systems.
The company has also identified longer local trips as an area where drones could play a role. DoorDash reported in July that more than 20% of its 2025 orders traveled three to five miles. Those orders took nearly 25% longer on average than shorter deliveries, partly because matching them with a Dasher took longer.
DoorDash Air therefore represents more than a new delivery aircraft. The company is building drones into the same platform that decides how millions of local orders move from merchants to customers. The Northern California pilot will provide an early test of how that end-to-end model works in restaurant operations.

DoorDash is launching new ways to use the local delivery platform, including text message ordering, drone deliveries, and retail returns. The new message ordering feature builds on capabilities that the Ask DoorDash AI chatbot introduced to the DoorDash app in June, allowing you to get recommendations and offload your browsing while skipping the app entirely.
“Ordering is now as easy as sending a text,” DoorDash said in its press release. “Whether you’re requesting a specific dish, asking for a local recommendation based on your mood, or telling DoorDash to ‘order my usual protein bowl to the office,’ it searches local spots, suggests a cart, and handles checkout right inside the text thread. It learns your preferences and remembers them for future orders.”
This is all just a preview for now because ordering by text isn’t available yet — iOS users in the US can join a waitlist from today to try the experience in beta. We’ve asked DoorDash for information about the rollout timeline and Android availability.
The first location for DoorDash Air, the company’s drone delivery service, has also been revealed. It’ll be piloted in an unspecified part of northern California with local food services, including Chipotle and Popeyes. DoorDash says around 80 percent of typical restaurant orders are “light and small enough for the aircraft to carry safely,” and that food arrives at customers’ doors within five minutes based on initial testing. DoorDash hasn’t announced when the drone deliveries will actually be available to consumers.
The limited capacity for drone orders means you probably won’t squeeze any massive takeout splurges in there. Image: DoorDash
Finally, a returns feature will be expanded across the US in November that allows customers to pay DoorDash couriers to send items back to local retailers. It’s only available in select cities right now, and costs $7.99 to schedule an eligible return. No box or shipping label is required — the item just gets collected from your door, taken back to the store, and then your return is processed for you.
The idea is to prevent you from missing the return window for unwanted products purchased on DoorDash due to other commitments that prevent you from shipping or taking it back yourself. TikTok announced its own version of this feature via UPS yesterday.

Home All News USA New York City Collects $131 Million From DoorDash for Delivery Workers Unfairly...
The New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) announced a historic $131.5 million enforcement action against DoorDash for systematic violations of the local Delivery Worker Laws.
The settlement will place more than $115 million directly into the pockets of delivery workers and pay for $16 million in civil penalties and costs. More than 260,000 workers were underpaid by DoorDash, including workers who were not paid at all, or were paid late for work they had already performed.
It’s the largest worker settlement in New York City history.
“DoorDash underpaid more than 260,000 workers, and today we are getting that money back,” said Mayor Mamdani. “When a worker earns a wage, they deserve to be paid that wage, on time and in full.”
He reminded the public that no corporation is above the law—especially when it earns $13.7 billion in revenue, like DoorDash did in 2025, a 28% increase compared to their 2024 revenue of $10.72 billion.
“Today, New York City’s delivery workers are showing that opaque algorithms will not have the final word when it comes to how much they are paid for the hard work they do,” said DCWP Commissioner Samuel A.A. Levine.
The settlement is about more than recovering money that workers are owed. It also puts in place a new monitoring system ensuring DoorDash follows the law going forward—one that gives workers a direct role in identifying violations and gives the City data it needs to act.
A Princeton University partner, the Workers’ Algorithm Observatory, will develop software that will allow the drivers to share their DoorDash trip and earnings data directly with the agency. It will allow DCWP to monitor DoorDash’s compliance with minimum pay, maximum trip distances, trip disclosures, pay transparency, and tip transparency.
DCWP’s citywide investigation began after dozens of workers filed reports with the Department.
The agency found that DoorDash failed to pay thousands of workers at all for work they had performed and failed to pay thousands more on time. These workers will receive compensation calculated at approximately 200% of the amount they were underpaid.
For example, a worker who was owed $1,000 but received no payment will receive $3,000. A worker who was paid $1,000 later than allowed under the law will receive $2,000.
Workers don’t even need to file a claim or submit evidence to receive payment. DCWP has identified all individuals owed money through its analysis of DoorDash’s records—and payments will be sent out this fall.
MORE IMPROVEMENTS FOR NYC: New York City is Putting ‘The Park’ Back in Park Avenue – And Adding a Protected Bike Lane (LOOK)
The case’s Settlement Administrator will send personalized emails to each worker who experienced an underpayment from April 22, 2022 to June 28, 2026. Workers will be able to choose between an electronic payment and a check by mail.
More details of the case is available at nyc.gov/doordash.
As part of the investigation, DCWP obtained terabytes of data from DoorDash, including billions of rows documenting the company’s treatment of delivery workers. DCWP’s Research and Analytics Division analyzed the data to identify more than 152 million individual payment transactions and 110 million working hours connected to the investigation.
DoorDash will be required to make software updates to prevent the company from offering a delivery to a worker in New York City unless that worker’s time is being recorded as compensable on-call time or trip time. The updates will also provide workers with additional information about their work time and pay and ensure DoorDash complies with the Minimum Pay Rule for “batched” trips, ending the unlawful practice of paying a lower rate for certain legs of a trip.
“Amidst a cost of living crisis, delivery workers deserve to rest assured that work completed means compensation earned,” said Council Member and Consumer and Worker Protection Chair Harvey Epstein.
The city passed a minimum wage law in 2021 which is adjusted annually for inflation and currently sits at $22.13 per hour.
“DoorDash thought they could shortchange their workers and get away with it,” said Council Member Sandy Nurse. “As DoorDash pulls in record profits, the workers who make them rich are entitled to their fair share.”

DoorDash expects to make 80 percent of the retail orders it handles eligible for Dasher Returns by the end of 2026.
DoorDash is expanding further into the fashion and apparel world, unveiling shoppers can now buy goods from Macy’s, Anthropologie, The North Face, Vans and Timberland directly from its retail marketplace.
The same-day delivery platform is also throwing its hat into the retail returns ecosystem with the launch of the Dasher Returns. Customers seeking to return an eligible retail purchase pay a flat fee of $7.99 for a courier to pick up the item from their door in as little as 30 minutes and return it to the store.

No box or prepaid label is required, DoorDash said. The service is available in select cities and is expected to expand across the U.S. in November.
The company revealed the product updates at its annual Dash Forward event Tuesday.
“This is what we mean by the mall in your pocket: the brands you already know and trust, on the shelf near you, delivered as easily as walking into the mall used to be. You can get Macy’s or Anthropologie in as little as an hour, and return it just as easily if it’s not right, no box, no label, back on the shelf and the money back in your pocket,” said Shanna Prevé, chief revenue officer at DoorDash in a statement. “For retailers, it means turning the stores they already have into a growth channel, not a warehouse three states away.”
At the event, Prevé told attendees DoorDash expects to make 80 percent of the retail orders it handles eligible for Dasher Returns by the end of 2026.
“Because that inventory goes back on the shelves today, Gap (a DoorDash partner) has a chance to resell it to another mom, and I get my refund in days, not weeks,” said Prevé.
Macy’s has partnered with DoorDash since 2020, with the department store enabling shoppers to select same-day delivery on its website via the platform’s Drive On-Demand service.
With the expanded collaboration, consumers can now find Macy’s assortment on the DoorDash Marketplace both online and in DoorDash’s mobile app, with the retailer offering two-hour delivery from more than 350 of its roughly 430 locations.
According to a report from The Wall Street Journal, Macy’s will make DoorDash’s delivery option more prominent on its own website. Previously, DoorDash branding was not included.
Anthropologie’s available assortment can be delivered from its more than 220 stores nationwide, while the three VF Corporation-owned brands can ship products from over 350 U.S. locations.
DoorDash, which is known largely for conducting restaurant and grocery delivery via a network of independent drivers, has scaled its retail footprint over the past year as it aims to tackle more of the last mile of the supply chain.
In 2026, retailers including Kohl’s, Carter’s, Costco, Gap, Anthropologie’s sister brand Urban Outfitters, Steve Madden, Dolce Vita and Hibbett have all joined DoorDash’s apparel marketplace. The companies joined a growing list including Old Navy, Pacsun, Dick’s Sporting Goods, Academy Sports + Outdoors, David’s Bridal and JD Sports, all of whom now can ship parcels same day from their stores.
Outside the Dasher Returns launch, returns for goods initially delivered via DoorDash are settled through each merchant’s own policy. To get a refund, shoppers have to initiate the return in the DoorDash app, take the item to the store, show an in-app return barcode and upload a photo of the return receipt.
DoorDash says that review process, including the refund, takes place in about four business days.
The terms are not uniform across the marketplace. For example, DoorDash offers Macy’s consumers free in-store only, 30-day returns. However, orders placed Oct. 5 through Dec. 31 can be returned through Jan. 31, 2027.
Anthropologie’s policy allows DoorDash purchases to be exchanged for the same product in a new size or color within 30 days at any of its stores. But the company explicitly states items are not eligible for refund or return.
Aside from the reveal of its new partnerships and returns offerings, DoorDash used the Dash Forward event to give more updates on its DoorDash Air drone delivery offering.
Pilot drone deliveries will begin in Northern California in partnership with national restaurant brands including Chipotle and Popeyes, the company said.
The delivery company has not revealed if any apparel or retail clients will be included in the pilots, and there has been no announcement when the drone deliveries will be available to consumers.
DoorDash says estimates from the initial tests indicate that deliveries arrive at the consumer’s door in under five minutes on average.
A week ahead of the event, DoorDash also introduced Brand Center, a platform giving merchant shelf-level visibility into their DoorDash performance. It surfaces on-shelf availability and out-of-stock trends across stores, shows what shoppers substitute when an item is unavailable and lets eligible brands edit product images, descriptions and categories directly.

DoorDash launches retail returns service, self-designed drones
DoorDash Air is a new drone delivery service that the company will operate using its own self-built aircraft rather than an outside supplier. (Photo: DoorDash)
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 10:03 AM PDT 5 min read
DoorDash is entering the reverse logistics market and leaning heavily into drone delivery, announcing on Wednesday that it has launched a new retail returns service and a custom-built drone delivery system for time-sensitive orders in another modal expansion of its last-mile logistics network.
They were among a series of product releases and enhancements, unveiled at a big user event, aimed at making shopping and ordering food, grocery and retail items more convenient.
The returns program is live in select cities and is expected to roll out nationwide in November using the same gig driver pool that delivers from stores to homes, the tech platform said. Consumers pay a flat $7.99 for Dasher Returns — no box or label required. DoorDash (NASDAQ: DASH) said drivers will pick up return orders in as fast as 30 minutes and return them to the store, which will process the return and issue a refund within days.
By offering returns, DoorDash is moving into a space that offers higher margins than store-to-door delivery and taking on parcel shipping incumbents like FedEx and UPS that are focusing more on returns than short-distance delivery in the B2C e-commerce market. FedEx last year began offering a lower cost version of its no-box, no-label returns to make it easier for customers to return unwanted merchandise, but the service requires consumers to drop off the goods at outlets such as FedEx Office and Kohl's store locations.
Earlier this year, Uber Eats introduced a service that allows customers to return goods ordered through its app for a fee.
But it's an open question whether consumers are willing to pay for returns when there is less urgency than with an inbound order and they can wait to drop it off at a store themselves for free.
"For retailers, it means turning the stores they already have into a growth channel, not a warehouse three states away," said Chief Revenue Officer Shanna Prevé in a news release.
Meanwhile, DoorDash has added to the growing number of retailers who have linked their product catalogs to its marketplace. Shoppers can now use the DoorDash app to order goods from Macy's, Anthropologie, The North Face, Vans and Timberland and receive fast delivery. Costco and Skims began delivery partnerships with DoorDash earlier this month.
DoorDash calls its retail product "Mall-in-Your-Pocket" because consumers can shop for apparel, beauty and home goods with fast delivery from hundreds of stores nationwide on one platform.
DoorDash also recently introduced new ways for retailers and brands to grow. Brand Center gives participating brands real-time visibility into inventory on store shelves and shopper substitution trends, helping them understand how their products are showing up in stores and what shoppers choose when an item is unavailable.
DoorDash also said it is investing in its own drone delivery operation, offering customers a faster delivery option from local restaurants and convenience stores.
The delivery platform's in-house robotics and automation division, DoorDash Labs, made the six-rotor drones on its own. Until now, DoorDash has relied on outside drone operators like Alphabet's Wing and Flytrex to conduct the actual aerial deliveries. Lowe's, for example, this month began a pilot program for drone delivery in North Carolina enabled by the DoorDash marketplace and Wing's small, unmanned aerial vehicles.
"We'll continue our partnership with third parties like Wing and Flytrex, but in the same way we use multiple delivery methods, having multiple drone delivery options adds resilience to our network and helps us better serve merchants and bring the benefits of drone delivery to more communities faster," said spokesman Eli Scheinholtz in an email exchange.
DoorDash said it closely consulted with businesses to design everything from packaging, to loading systems and ground handoffs. It is building an array of loading options designed to fit into existing business operations and make drone delivery feasible for local businesses of all sizes.
About 80% of typical DoorDash restaurant orders are light and small enough for the aircraft to carry safely.
"Any local business should be able to reach consumers by air. We built the whole system so that they can deliver by air without being disruptive to how they run their business," said Harrison Shih, head of DoorDash Air, in the announcement.
Trial flights are underway in Northern California with national brands Chipotle and Popeyes, and local restaurants. Delivery times have averaged less than five minutes so far, DoorDash said.
Customers can choose on the app whether their order is delivered by a driver, its self-designed small robot or a drone. An autonomous system uses smart routing, incorporating factors like weather, flight range, and ground traffic to narrow down which orders actually make sense to send by air. Using the app, customers can select whether a driver, a Dot robot or a drone is the best delivery option.
The drone's cruising noise is similar to that of a passing car. Orders are picked up and lowered to the ground with a winch, with a backup option to safely lower the aircraft to the ground in rare events, DoorDash said. Amazon drones, by contrast, drop boxes at their destination from about 13 feet in the air.
In other news, DoorDash also introduced text ordering, allowing customers to simply send a text describing what they want from a restaurant or grocery store without the need to fiddle with an app or browser.
Why It Matters: DoorDash is a giant platform that is leveraging its technology to push more and more into retail parcel delivery and becoming a competitor to other courier companies.

Inside DoorDash’s Push to Connect Every Restaurant Channel
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 9:04 AM PDT 4 min read
This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt.
DashOS is meant to link marketplace discovery with future transactions.
DoorDash wants to become more than a delivery marketplace for restaurants.
Its new DashOS platform connects ordering, reservations, loyalty, customer data, and marketing. The goal is to help restaurants recognize the same guest across delivery, direct ordering, and dine-in visits, then use that information to bring the customer back.
That is difficult for many operators today. Guests move easily between channels, but their activity often lands in separate systems. One person can appear to be several unrelated customers, leaving restaurants without a clear picture of what led to another purchase.
Restaurants also have to oversee numerous technology products in addition to running their kitchens and dining rooms. DoorDash data shows 40 percent of surveyed U.S. operators use four to five systems, and 83 percent believe better-connected technology would improve profitability.
"The idea is really to become the growth partner for merchants, period, and be the one-stop shop for merchants to look to when they say I wanna grow," says Parisa Sadrzadeh, DoorDash's vice president of strategy and operations.
DoorDash introduced DashOS during its Dash Forward 2026 event. The platform connects DoorDash Marketplace with the company's direct ordering, loyalty, reservation, and marketing products.
Customers must opt into a restaurant's loyalty program or agree to share their information for marketing. Once they do, the restaurant can see eligible activity across the DoorDash products it uses and communicate with that customer directly.
DoorDash sees its marketplace as the starting point for many of those relationships. A customer might discover a restaurant through delivery, return through its website, and later visit in person. DashOS is designed to connect those transactions instead of treating each one as a separate relationship.
The early loyalty results provide DoorDash's clearest evidence for the model. More than one in five customers who visit the DoorDash page of a participating restaurant enroll in its loyalty program. Those members order 1.8 times as often and spend approximately 1.75 times as much per person as customers who have not enrolled.
DashOS can use purchasing history to recommend menu items and support marketing through email, text messages and push notifications. Campaigns can run automatically for restaurants without dedicated marketing employees, or operators can customize them.
The information can follow customers to a restaurant's direct ordering site. Once logged in, a customer can see previous DoorDash orders, receive recommendations, and use saved payment information. DoorDash can also provide delivery for the direct order.
Reservations are another piece of the customer record. DoorDash said AI-powered recommendations increased total bookings by more than 15 percent in early tests. SevenRooms marketing products using blinded, aggregated DoorDash Marketplace information have produced more than $150 million in restaurant sales this year. DoorDash acquired SevenRooms in 2025.
The platform works with technology restaurants already use. DoorDash is expanding connections with Clover, Qu, Checkmate, Chowly, Deliverect, Stream and UrbanPiper. Starting in 2027, more than 80,000 restaurants using those providers are expected to gain access to SevenRooms customer profiles, online ordering, in-store rewards and omnichannel loyalty products.
DoorDash still has work to do to make the products operate as one system. The company has connected its merchant portal more closely with its customer relationship software and plans more automation.
"The idea is to simplify this into one platform," Sadrzadeh says. "We need to continue to improve it and continue to simplify it."
DashOS is one piece of DoorDash's effort to play a larger role in local commerce. The company also introduced a service that lets customers order through text messages.
U.S. consumers using iPhones can join a waitlist for the beta. A customer can text DoorDash with a specific request, ask for a local recommendation, or request a usual order. The system searches nearby restaurants, builds a suggested cart, and handles checkout inside the conversation. It can also remember preferences and order modifications.
The service builds on Ask DoorDash, the company's in-app ordering assistant. DoorDash said customers have used the assistant to discover more than 40,000 restaurants. Nearly half of restaurant orders placed through it went to businesses those customers had not tried previously.
DoorDash also introduced DoorDash Air, an autonomous delivery system scheduled to begin pilot service in Northern California with Chipotle, Popeyes and local restaurants.
The company designed the aircraft, packaging, and loading process using historical order information and existing kitchen workflows. Roughly 80 percent of typical restaurant orders on DoorDash are light and small enough for the aircraft to carry safely, depending on travel distance and operating conditions.
Early tests produced average travel times of less than five minutes from a restaurant to a customer's door. DoorDash's Autonomous Delivery Platform chooses whether a driver, Dot delivery robot, or drone is the best option for each eligible order. The decision accounts for distance, weight, weather, traffic, and kitchen preparation time.
The Dash Forward event also included retail returns, AI assistance for drivers, and a connector that can bring DoorDash ordering into compatible workplace AI products.
